section_summary: This section centers on the January 1940 Shizuoka fire, documenting the safety of American residents, Japanese relief efforts, physical destruction, and insurance losses, together with newspaper clippings and a detailed consular registration list. It also contains an extensive report on drought damage to the Kyushu rice crop and relief measures in Nagasaki Prefecture, plus a March 1940 analysis of Japan’s related coal and electric-power shortages. Later-filed material covers proposed American Red Cross assistance after a 1941 typhoon, wartime relief and property questions, earthquake reporting, and the December 1944 Tokaido earthquake; a few apparently incidental documents concern wheat sales and Japanese intelligence activity.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting the safety of Americans after the Shizuoka fire
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports that registered American citizens in Shizuoka were believed safe after the January fire.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports only two registered American families of Japanese ancestry lived in the devastated Shizuoka district; the Kageyama children are safe, Teiko Kobayashi unfound but believed safe, others undamaged.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Yokohama despatch no. 613
subfiles.about: Summarizes the consul’s final report concerning American citizens affected by the Shizuoka fire.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern note: the Yokohama consul accounted for all American citizens in Shizuoka during the fire, so no American relief was needed.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 613: Fire at Shizuoka City, Shizuoka Prefecture
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Provides the final accounting of Teiko Kobayashi and commends the MacKenzies’ assistance.
subfiles.summary: Police inquiries established that Teiko Kobayashi was no longer living at the registered Morishita-chō address when the house burned, and all its occupants had been accounted for. Boyce concludes that all registered Americans were safe and formally credits Duncan and Emily MacKenzie for making the rapid welfare survey possible.

subfiles.title: Relief Measures in Nagasaki Prefecture Necessitated by Drought Damage to Rice Crop
subfiles.from: Arthur F. Tower, American Consul, Nagasaki
subfiles.about: Analyzes the 1939 Kyushu drought, rice-production economics, and relief policies in Nagasaki Prefecture.
subfiles.summary: Tower describes extreme water shortages and severe rice-crop losses in Nagasaki, Fukuoka, and Saga prefectures, comparing 1939 production costs with controlled retail prices. Relief measures included seasonal day nurseries, soldiers’ furloughs, student labor, subsidized fodder purchases, and road-building projects. He also considers possible direct compensation for rice producers and appends detailed national rice-production costs for 1938.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 605: Fire at Shizuoka City, Shizuoka Prefecture
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Gives a detailed firsthand report on the Shizuoka fire, American residents, and Japanese relief operations.
subfiles.summary: Boyce describes the destruction of much of Shizuoka’s business district and a working-class residential area, with estimated losses of as much as ¥75 million but few casualties. He recounts his journey from Yokohama, the search for registered Americans, the destruction of several families’ homes, and the safe location of the Kageyama family. Japanese authorities rapidly supplied food, medical care, and shelter, while Boyce brought canned goods and expressed sympathy to the governor and mayor.

subfiles.title: True reading of telegram sent January 19, 1940
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Preserves the official text of Boyce’s telegram on the safety of Americans in Shizuoka.
subfiles.summary: True reading of the January 19, 1940 telegram: only two of 54 registered American residents were in the devastated district; Kageyama children safe, Kobayashi children believed safe, others undamaged.

subfiles.title: Japan Times & Mail clipping: Homeless from Fire Monday in Shizuoka City
subfiles.about: Reports the scale, course, and immediate relief response to the Shizuoka conflagration.
subfiles.summary: Japan Times & Mail: about 6,700 houses burned and 36,900 made homeless in a thirteen-hour Shizuoka fire with two deaths, destroying the station and commercial center amid rapid relief.

subfiles.title: Japan Advertiser clippings on the Shizuoka fire
subfiles.about: Describes devastation, survivor morale, reconstruction, and government relief after the Shizuoka fire.
subfiles.summary: Japan Advertiser clippings compare ruined Shizuoka to wartime Shanghai, noting calm refugees and quick reconstruction; wind, narrow streets and drought spread the fire; agencies supplied rice, shelter and labor.

subfiles.title: Registrations—Shizuoka City
subfiles.about: Lists registered American residents of Shizuoka and records their families, addresses, occupations, and fire damage.
subfiles.summary: Shizuoka registration list of missionaries, tea company staff, students and American families of Japanese ancestry, noting destroyed or spared homes and moves to Yui, Numazu, the US or Formosa.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 606: Fire in Shizuoka City, Shizuoka Prefecture
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Forwards a British consular memorandum on insurance losses from the Shizuoka fire.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 606: Boyce encloses a British Consulate memorandum estimating insurance losses from the Shizuoka fire.

subfiles.title: Shizuoka Fire—Insurance Companies’ Losses
subfiles.about: Estimates Japanese and foreign insurers’ liabilities arising from the Shizuoka fire.
subfiles.summary: Shizuoka fire insured losses about ¥20 million, ten percent borne by foreign companies since Japanese discouraged reinsurance; lists estimated liabilities for several insurers.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum: Shipment
subfiles.to: Department of State files; copies to Hornbeck and Acheson
subfiles.about: Records Fred Mallon’s inquiry about sudden Japanese purchases of American wheat and flour.
subfiles.summary: Mallon reports new Japanese wheat and flour orders and Japanese, German and Italian funds leaving the US, asking about future embargoes protecting contracts; Hamilton declined to predict an embargo and asked continued reporting.

subfiles.title: Special Division referral of typhoon-relief proposal
subfiles.about: Requests Far Eastern Affairs’ view on referring Arthur Paterson’s Japanese typhoon-relief proposal to the American Red Cross.
subfiles.summary: Special Division notes Paterson's typhoon-relief proposal has political implications and asks Far Eastern Affairs whether to refer it to the American Red Cross.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs recommendation on Paterson’s proposal
subfiles.about: Recommends routine referral of Arthur Paterson’s typhoon-relief suggestion to the American Red Cross.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs proposes sending Paterson's letter to the Red Cross, advising him, and acknowledging his compliments on the Secretary's statesmanship.

subfiles.title: Arthur E. Paterson to Secretary Hull proposing aid for Japanese typhoon victims
subfiles.about: Suggests humanitarian American assistance for Japanese typhoon sufferers during a period of political tension.
subfiles.summary: Paterson proposes Red Cross aid for Japanese typhoon victims as a show of American humanitarianism while defending rights in East Asia, and praises Hull.

subfiles.title: Reply to Arthur E. Paterson
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Paterson’s relief proposal and reports its referral to the American Red Cross.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Paterson the pertinent part of his letter went to the American Red Cross and conveys the Secretary's appreciation.

subfiles.title: Referral of Paterson’s typhoon-relief proposal to the American Red Cross
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: L. N. Mitchell, American Red Cross
subfiles.about: Transmits Arthur Paterson’s suggestion that the American Red Cross aid Japanese typhoon victims.
subfiles.summary: Green sends the Red Cross the relevant part of Paterson's October 3 letter and notes Paterson was advised.

subfiles.title: War Department G-2 letter of transmittal
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.to: A. A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards military-intelligence communications for State Department information and possible action.
subfiles.summary: War Department G-2 transmits two confidential items, one on Sasaki and one on a Sheffield, Texas mercantile company; second enclosure missing.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence summary concerning Sasaki
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, U.S. War Department
subfiles.to: Intelligence distribution and Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports allegations that Sasaki collected funds under Japanese naval direction and was transferred to Washington.
subfiles.summary: Intelligence summary: Sasaki, executive of the Gardena Nikkai branch and fundraiser for Japan's war needs, moved to Washington under Japanese Embassy orders; State registration status unknown.

subfiles.title: American Red Cross response concerning aid after the Japanese typhoon
subfiles.from: L. N. Mitchell, American Red Cross
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the American Red Cross would not initiate typhoon relief in Japan without a request or evidence of unmet need.
subfiles.summary: American Red Cross says foreign disaster aid normally follows a request from the affected country's Red Cross for emergencies beyond local resources; none was requested and time had passed, so no unilateral action.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Red Cross personnel aboard exchange vessels
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram concerning space for accredited Red Cross personnel on exchange vessels.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: telegram 405 saying exchange vessels could also carry accredited International Red Cross Committee or other Red Cross personnel.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on earthquake information from observatories
subfiles.about: References a request for transmitting earthquake data from Australia, New Zealand, and England.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: letter requesting arrangements for earthquake information from Melbourne or Sydney, Wellington and Kew observatories.

subfiles.title: Ella W. Morton’s protest concerning reported milk shipments to Japanese children
subfiles.about: Protests a rumor that milk was being sent to Japanese children while American children lacked milk.
subfiles.summary: Gold Star mother Ella Morton asks why milk was reportedly supplied to Japanese children when American children could not obtain it, calling it an insult.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Ella W. Morton
subfiles.from: Eldred D. Kuppinger, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Denies the rumor that the United States was sending milk to Japanese children.
subfiles.summary: Kuppinger replies, via White House referral, that the Department knew of no such milk shipments and none was contemplated.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of International Red Cross report on Yokohama Internment Camp No. 2
subfiles.to: Marc Peter, International Committee of the Red Cross
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of a Geneva telegram concerning an International Red Cross visit to a Yokohama internment camp.
subfiles.summary: Green thanks Peter for his June 10 letter enclosing a Geneva telegram on an International Red Cross delegate's visit to Yokohama Internment Camp No. 2.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on proposed Swiss occupancy of the Yokohama consulate
subfiles.from: Leland Harrison, U.S. mission in Switzerland
subfiles.about: References a proposal that Swiss and Red Cross personnel occupy the vacant American consular property in Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Swiss occupancy of the vacant Yokohama consulate would block Japanese refugee use and house the Swiss foreign-interests section and Red Cross delegate Fritz Paravicini, per Camille Gorgé.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the desirability of Swiss and Red Cross occupancy
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State (Benninghoff)
subfiles.about: References an internal memorandum supporting Swiss and Red Cross use of the American consular building in Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Swiss and Red Cross occupancy of the Yokohama building was considered highly desirable; original memorandum filed elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note approving occupancy of the Yokohama consular building
subfiles.about: References instructions approving Swiss and International Red Cross occupancy of the Yokohama consulate.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: telegram approving use of the American consular building at Yokohama by the Swiss Foreign Interests Section and Red Cross delegation.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram reporting the Tokaido earthquake
subfiles.about: Relays a Pravda report of a December 7 earthquake in Japan’s Tokaido region.
subfiles.summary: Moscow telegram: Pravda of December 10 reported an earthquake in Japan's Tokaido area on December 7.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs analysis of Japan’s coal and electric-power shortages
subfiles.about: Analyzes the institutional, industrial, coal-supply, and drought causes of Japan’s electric-power shortage.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern analysis attributes Japan's coal and power shortage to underinvestment before state control, rapid industrial expansion, poor coordination and low rainfall, showing industrial ambitions exceeding the economy's capacity.
